newsitem.title: USA: Orlando-Orange Cty, Fla., authority seen strong.
newsitem.headline: Orlando-Orange Cty, Fla., authority seen strong.

text.p: Florida's Orlando-Orange County Expressway Authority has seen strong revenue growth and streamlined operations and could be a candidate for a bond rating upgrade, PaineWebber Inc said in a report Monday.

"In our opinion, a rating upgrade is possible provided that the authority continues to exhibit favorable financial operations and that the capital improvement program does not project material dilution of security through additional indebtedness," the report by Senior Research Analyst Jeff Lipton said.
The authority's senior lien bonds are rated single-A by Standard & Poor's Corp and Fitch Investors Service. Its junior lien bonds are rated A-minus by S&P and single-A by Fitch.
The authority system consists of three primarily limited-access toll roads -- the Beeline Expressway, the East-West Expressway and the Central Florida Greenway.

PaineWebber said much of the authority's strong revenue growth in the past four years was due to better than projected traffic volume. But it also praised the authority's "very capable management" which is oriented towards containing costs and streamlining operations.

The authority's privatization of toll collection operations has yielded about $1 million in labor cost savings. Its adaptation of an electronic collection and billing system has produced better than expected results, accounting for 28 percent of system transactions and revenues.
The report said the authority is vulnerable to recessionary pressures because the Orlando area depends heavily on tourism.

But both its senior and junior lien bonds have addedsecurity via an interlocal agreement with Orange County. The county has pledged up to 80 percent of revenues from its two-cent gasoline tax if toll revenues, minus operating expenses, are inadequate to pay debt service. That tax raised $5.8 million in fiscal 1985.
"We note that the authority has not used gas tax moneys since 1978," the report said.
Both senior and junior lien bonds maintain debt service reserves funded at maximum future debt service, the report said.
The authority also has absolute toll rate setting oversight. It raised tolls in 1980, 1987 and 1990, but lowered some rates in 1992.

The authority saw a dip in traffic in the early 1990s because of the reccession and the Gulf War, which impacted commuter and tourist travel in the Orlando area. Since then it has seen steady increases in traffic and toll revenues.
Traffic for the first nine months of fiscal 1997, through March 30, was up 12.7 percent over the same period last year. Toll revenues grew by 13.3 percent during the period.
Much of the latter was due to the 22.4 percent revenue growth on the Greenway Expresway, which has contributed increasingly to system revenues since the Southern Connector segment opened in 1993.
The East-West Expressway, which saw 10.8 percent revenue growth for the nine months, remains the most actively traveled road and accounts for about half of the system's total revenues.
Debt service coverage for fiscal 1997 is projected at 1.53x without county gas tax revenues and and 1.65x with the gas tax, the report said.
